coldRead.icp: Nurse manager at a 25-bed rural Texas CAH who builds a 12-hour night rotation for 6 to 8 night nurses and keeps getting 'one night, then off' complaints; reading once on a phone

undefinedTerms: governing bodies (whose fatigue and safety guidelines apply to a Texas CAH?)
rotating schedules (does NIOSH's short-run advice apply to permanent night staff?)
mondayActions: Mark every off, on, off pattern in each night nurse's row on the current schedule
Try moving each island night next to that nurse's other nights, or to a nurse whose run it extends
Set a rule for the next build: nights in runs of two or three, two days off after three 12-hour nights
On every callout, check each candidate's day before and day after, and say plainly when the ask is an island
Keep a running note of who covers island nights to spot the one nurse who always says yes
blockedActions: Rebuild next month's 4-week rotation for 6 to 8 night nurses in runs: no worked pattern showing how runs tile across 28 nights at the unit's nightly headcount
Move an island night next to the nurse's other nights: the post says the same gaps stay covered but never shows who now covers the vacated night
Handle islands that exist because the nurse requested the surrounding days off, or prefers single nights: the likely source of the complaints is not addressed
Act on 'ask the nurse before the schedule posts': ask what, and what to do if she says no
Extend a run on a callout safely: 'if rest allows' gives no limit and conflicts with the three-night cap

sections.heading: What Is an Island Shift in Nursing?
sections.notes: Includes the intro. Reread: 'then doing the same thing again on Friday' (is Friday also an island? Saturday is never stated). 'adapted from ergonomic guidance by the shift-work researchers Knauth and Hornberger' and the journal name are skipped as noise.

sections.heading: Why Are Island Shifts Harder on Night Nurses?
sections.notes: Reread: 'In an island shift, every night worked is one.' An island shift is one night, so 'every night' and 'one' (= first night back) both stall. Same phrasing in Key Takeaways and FAQ.

sections.heading: Why Do Island Shifts Show Up on Small Hospital Schedules?
sections.notes: Reread: '115 of the 182 nurses ... 29 of the 255 island shifts' then told the counts do not transfer to 12-hour units, so why read them. 'Island nights were the rarest kind' cuts against the night-nurse thrust. Evidence is Korean and Australian large hospitals; the small-hospital answer is one sentence plus a link. Attention dips here.

sections.heading: How Do You Schedule Island Shifts Out of a Night Rotation?
sections.notes: Reread: 'Both columns cover the same three nights with the same nurse' (table shows Tue-Wed-Thu vs Tue-Fri-Sat, not the same nights). Reread: 'splits the nurse's days off into two short stretches' (Wednesday after a Tuesday night is a sleep day, not a day off). 'If neither works, ask the nurse' has no object: ask what?

sections.heading: How Do You Avoid an Island Shift When Covering a Callout?
sections.notes: Reread: 'A nurse finishing a run of nights can add one more if rest allows' makes a fourth night, against the three-night cap two sections earlier; 'if rest allows' has no number.

sections.heading: Does SimpleScheduleAI Prevent Island Shifts?
sections.notes: Answers 'Not directly' up front (good). Reread: 'What the schedule you approve does respect is the fatigue limits next to that pattern.' Reread: 'A count of zero days in a row means the nurse is coming off a day off.' 'schedule record' / 'per-nurse night count ... on request' reads like a product spec. Four paragraphs of what the product does not do plus a four-link 'More on the service' list: skimmed, not read.

sections.heading: Frequently Asked Questions
sections.notes: Texas Q is the most useful new line in the piece: a posted island is not Chapter 258 overtime.
